title: Trump Rolls Back Fuel Economy Rules, Sparking Debate Over Cars and Climate
summary:
President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that he is rolling back fuel economy standards adopted under former President Joe Biden, calling the previous rules an "EV mandate" that drove up costs for carmakers and consumers.

In a social media post, Trump said the new standards would "TERMINATE" Biden's "EV mandate" and "take the waste out of building cars in America." He promised "LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car." The changes are part of a broader effort to reverse Biden-era policies that supported lower-emission vehicles.

But there's a catch: there is no federal law or guideline that requires Americans to buy electric vehicles or bans the sale of gasoline-powered cars. The term "EV mandate" is a political phrase, not a legal one. The actual rules at the center are Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, established by Congress in 1975. They require automakers to meet average fuel economy targets across all cars and light trucks they sell. A brand that sells an inefficient vehicle must also sell a more efficient one to comply.

Under rules finalized by the Biden administration in 2024, the required fleetwide fuel economy was scheduled to rise from 39.1 miles per gallon to about 50.4 mpg by 2031. Biden officials said the measures would reduce fuel consumption and emissions to combat climate change while helping motorists save money at the pump. Carmakers responded by ramping up EV production to help meet the requirements.

Trump did not provide details on the new standards. But in December 2025, he proposed setting the industry fleetwide average for light-duty vehicles at roughly 34.5 mpg by 2031 — more than 30 percent lower than the Biden-era rule. The Republican-controlled Congress also gutted consumer tax incentives for electric vehicles last year as part of Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy reposted Trump's announcement and said a formal announcement would be "COMING MONDAY." Al Jazeera reached out to the White House for comment. The debate highlights a growing gap between US policy and global trends favoring electric vehicles, with automakers caught between changing regulations and consumer demand.
why_it_matters: Fuel economy rules shape what kinds of cars get built for the next decade, which affects the air people breathe, the price of driving and the jobs tied to car factories; the debate also shows how sharply US policy can swing between administrations, leaving carmakers, workers and buyers to plan around rules that may not survive the next election.

background_read: Fuel economy rules go back to the 1970s oil crisis, when an oil embargo sent gasoline prices soaring and Congress responded with the Corporate Average Fuel Economy law in 1975 — the same law at the centre of today's fight. Because the rules cover a company's whole fleet, carmakers can keep selling big trucks as long as they also sell efficient models.

The standards have swung back and forth with each administration, so carmakers have learned to design vehicles that can satisfy more than one set of rules. In the US, California has long held a special permission to set stricter pollution rules than the federal government, and more than a dozen other states follow California's lead — a dispute that keeps returning to court.

Electric vehicles have also become a global industry. China and the European Union sell far more EVs than the United States, and several countries have set dates to stop selling new gasoline cars, which is part of the gap between US policy and worldwide trends. In the US, the rules are enforced by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (the federal agency that writes vehicle safety and mileage rules), while the Environmental Protection Agency handles related pollution limits.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — cheaper cars and fewer burdens
perspectives.description: Supporters of the rollback argue the stricter targets pushed carmakers to build expensive electric models that many buyers did not want, adding cost to every vehicle sold. In their view, loosening the fleetwide average lowers sticker prices, protects American manufacturing jobs and lets the market — not regulators — decide how quickly drivers go electric.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — climate and public health costs
perspectives.description: Opponents say weaker mileage rules mean more gasoline burned, more planet-warming emissions and higher long-term fuel bills for families, even if cars cost less up front. They also point out that the 'EV mandate' label describes something that never existed in law, and warn that carmakers who slow their electric plans will fall behind competitors abroad.

Analysts note that US fuel economy standards have repeatedly tightened under one administration and eased under the next, and that carmakers plan years ahead using averages across many possible futures. The deeper structural fact is that a fleetwide average lets companies keep selling large, inefficient vehicles as long as efficient ones balance them out — which is why the rules have always been a fight over the mix of cars on the lot.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — where the industry goes next
perspectives.description: The open questions are what the final numbers will be, whether California and other states can keep stricter rules of their own, and how a global shift toward electric vehicles will affect US factories either way. Automakers are hedging: designing platforms that can carry either a gasoline engine or a battery, so they can adjust when the rules change again.
